query: For a FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy used as a thin coating on a conventional metal substrate, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs overall wear resistance and microscopic deformation during sliding in the intended high-temperature operating regime? Define a controlled change relative to a baseline coating condition, predict the corresponding directional changes in wear and deformation, state the regime in which those predictions should hold, identify supporting prior evidence, and specify a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: The wear resistance and microscopic deformation of a FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy thin coating on a conventional metal substrate during sliding in the high-temperature operating regime are governed by the formation of a stable, coherent oxide layer at the surface, which acts as a protective barrier against wear and deformation.
generation.material_initial_state: FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy thin coating on a conventional metal substrate, with a surface roughness of 0.1 μm and a coating thickness of 10 μm
generation.intervention: Increase in coating thickness by 50% (from 10 μm to 15 μm) through controlled deposition
generation.conditions: High-temperature operating regime (500°C - 700°C), sliding speed of 1 m/s, and a normal load of 10 N
generation.structural_mediator: Stable, coherent oxide layer at the surface
generation.mechanism: Formation of a protective oxide layer through thermally-activated diffusion and reaction of metal ions with oxygen, leading to reduced wear and deformation
generation.predicted_outcome: A 25% increase in wear resistance (measured as a decrease in wear rate from 10^-4 mm^3/Nm to 7.5^-4 mm^3/Nm) and a 30% reduction in microscopic deformation (measured as a decrease in deformation depth from 5 μm to 3.5 μm) compared to the baseline coating condition
generation.baseline: 10 μm thick FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy coating
generation.boundary: High-temperature operating regime (500°C - 700°C), sliding speed of 1 m/s, and a normal load of 10 N
generation.uncertainty: The actual wear resistance and deformation may vary depending on the specific coating deposition method, substrate material, and testing conditions. Additionally, the formation of the oxide layer may be influenced by factors such as humidity, atmospheric pressure, and surface contamination.

falsification_experiment.design: Sliding wear tests with integrated molecular dynamics simulations to investigate the formation of the oxide layer and its effect on wear resistance and deformation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the wear rate increases by more than 10% (from 10^-4 mm^3/Nm to 1.1^-4 mm^3/Nm) or the deformation depth increases by more than 15% (from 5 μm to 5.75 μm) with the increased coating thickness, the hypothesis is falsified.
